# binding-symbols: a global the C contract lets a program set is mutable, whatever its known users do

Status: `open`: the change is crustify `30fa33f` on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/global-the-program-may-set`, made on
2026-11-14 at the user's direction after the triage of open proposals, awaiting its review.

Goal: Safety, its soundness measure.

## Signal

A finding a how-to rule should have prevented (`evolution` §2, a rule the how-to skills
lack). Planner run 1 (`25b3fe2`) planned glibc's `stderr` as "a 'static shared handle: no
C of either parent writes it, and its storage (_IO_2_1_stderr_) is static". Wave 4's
binder bound it so, as a safe `stderr() -> FileRef<'static>`. Its doc listed what the
borrow assumes of the whole program: nothing assigns `stderr`, closes its stream or unlocks
it. Its justification was that neither glibc's routines nor the parents' C do. The module
pass found the contract broken through safe code. glibc's manual offers `fclose (stdout);
stdout = fopen (…);` as the way to redirect a standard stream, and a kept handle then
outlives the stream `fclose` freed: a heap-use-after-free under ASan
(`crustify/reviews/modules/libc/libio/stdio.c/wave-4/batch-1/contracts/ffi_import/stderr-lends-a-static-stream-the-program-may-close/`).

The Globals section's split is by "every C access", which both the planner and the binder
read as the accesses in the code the campaign can see. For a wrapper, that is never all of
the program. A library cannot see its consumers' C, and a parent campaign's C is not its
consumers' C either: libgit2 is a library too.

## Destination

The spec: `binding-symbols` §2, Globals.

## Change

After the list of access disciplines, add:

> The accesses that decide are those the C declaration's contract allows, not those the
> campaign's C makes: a global the library documents as one a program may set, such as
> libc's standard streams, `environ` or `optarg`, is otherwise mutable however the code
> the campaign sees uses it, since the crate cannot see every program it is linked into.
> Where it holds a pointer, what it points to may be freed by the C that reassigns it, so
> a safe accessor never lends what it names beyond the call: the accessor is `unsafe`,
> its caller vouching for the lifetime it chooses, or a safe operation reads the global
> and uses what it names within one call, as the C expression does, holding the lock C
> takes there.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a global's access discipline follows from what its C declaration's contract allows, so one a program may set is otherwise mutable and a safe accessor never lends what it points to beyond a call | `glibc-crustify`, `global-the-program-may-set` | crustify `30fa33f` | "every C access" was read as the campaign's C: a safe handle to a standard stream outlived the program's `fclose`, a use-after-free from safe code | a `ub` finding on a safe accessor of a global a program outside the campaign's C may set or free | watched |

## Validation

The rerun is the module pass's fix (`wave-4/batch-1`). Under the rule, `stderr` is bound
as `unsafe fn stderr<'a>() -> FileRef<'a>`. The reproducer's safe step then fails to
compile (`E0133`), which `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/stdio_stderr_is_lent_by_no_safe_code.rs`
keeps. The workspace's tests pass plain and under ASan and TSan, and Miri passes per test
binary.

Plan side: `planner/run-2` (2026-11-13) withdrew run 1's shape for `stderr` as a plan
correction
(`crustify/reviews/planner/modules/stderr-planned-as-a-safe-static-handle/report.md`).
The plan now names the entity alone, and leaves a global's discipline to this section of
`binding-symbols`. `decomposition` states no access discipline, so the proposal asks
nothing of it.

## Review

Not reviewed.

# Lessons of glibc-crustify

Rules that hold for this campaign alone, as `evolution`'s Lessons section describes. Every
run reads them before its first step.

## A batch's gates run with no build variant

**Rule.** libc is the system's, so `build.json` has no variants, and this tree has no
`cargo-variant` script. A batch runs its gates directly, each build in a target dir of its
own under `crustify/tmp/`:

- campaign mode: `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=<plain | asan-ubsan | tsan>` set on every
  `cargo` command that builds the tests, which then regenerate the bindings and check them
  against the committed ones;
- format: `cargo +<the workspace's nightly> fmt --all -- --check`, since `rustfmt.toml`
  uses nightly-only options;
- ASan: on that nightly, `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, with
  `RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"`, and the same flags in
  `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, without which the doctests fail to link against the ASan runtime; TSan:
  the same with `-Zsanitizer=thread` and `-Zbuild-std`. They instrument the Rust alone,
  since the system's glibc is not instrumented, so TSan sees no race inside glibc. The host
  has no `llvm-symbolizer` on its `PATH`, so a sanitizer trace a report carries is
  symbolized with `ASAN_OPTIONS=external_symbolizer_path=/usr/bin/addr2line`;
- coverage: Rust only, measured as the parent's `crustify/scripts/coverage/baseline.sh`
  does, over a scratch copy without `c/`. Its `report.py` rejects the scope, since
  `llvm-cov` prints this tree's file names relative to `src/`, so the `TOTAL` line is read
  from `llvm-cov report` itself. The compile-fail suite fails in the marked copy, which
  only a nightly builds, and it covers nothing. Its `mark.py` misses a test item whose
  attributes span lines, so a test module's `#[expect]` is kept on one line, and the copy
  holds the tree's package, or the script measures the workspace that encloses it
  (`crustify/evolution/coverage-marking-misses-multiline-attributes`);
- a wave's and a module's end gates: `testing-gates`' `end-gates`, with `--stages
  plain,asan-ubsan,tsan,miri` and with `--runner` set to a script in `crustify/tmp/`. Given
  `<variant> <cargo args>`, the script runs `cargo` with the flags above, adding
  `--target-dir` under the worktree's `crustify/tmp/` so that every snapshot reuses one
  build per variant. Miri takes `--stage-env miri:CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=plain` and
  `--stage-env miri:CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<worktree>/crustify/tmp/target-miri`.

**Evidence.** wave-2/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/genops.c`) worked these out by hand.
wave-2/batch-1/run-1, its module pass, wrote the `end-gates` runner by hand too.
wave-3/batch-0/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`) found that the `struct_tm_h` doctest fails to
link under ASan without `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, and passes with it.
wave-4/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/stdio.c`) found the doctests failing to link under ASan with
`RUSTFLAGS` alone (`undefined symbol: __asan_init`), and passing with `RUSTDOCFLAGS`.
wave-4/batch-1/run-1, its module pass, found its reproducer's ASan trace printed as bare
addresses, and symbolized through `addr2line`.
wave-5/batch-1/run-1, its module pass, measured `genops.rs`' test module as covered code
under a multi-line `#[expect]`, and kept it on one line.

**Scope.** Every batch until the tree gets a variant script.

providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the

wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that

## 1. Goals

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|

| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. A change is finished once its proposal names its commit. A finished
change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on
the fix rather than around it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- the row its proposal drafts for the record, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes, names a recurrence
  signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. A rebase of a change to
the text of skills, agents or templates alone, no script or program among its files, is the
exception, where each file the commit changes is the same in the rebased commit and its
parent as in the reviewed commit and its parent: the review then read the same diff against
the same text. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided changes no rule and is not reviewed: a row of the index,
a status of the record, or a proposal's status, verdict and review. A row of the record is
reviewed in its proposal, with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.

The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;
- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
  skills included;
- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

# Binding symbols

How a scheduled C symbol becomes a safe Rust binding: the symbol route, which follows
[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section and reaches the types
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md) binds. [`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md) starts from it.

## 1. Functions

A function is bound as a `pub fn`; it is a `pub unsafe fn` only when no safe type-level
contract can express its caller obligation. Its FFI call, and the raw pointers it
reconstructs for it, sit in its module's `ffi_import` region, as the
[conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes.

Its signature follows the analysis's findings, each argument and return taking the safe
form of what it names:

- **Out-parameters.** A pointer the function only writes through, to hand back a result,
  is part of the return, several of them a tuple, present only in the outcome in which the
  function writes it.
- **Buffers.** A pointer and the count that bounds it are one slice, the count taken from
  it; a buffer the function fills returns the part it filled.
- **Strings.** A NUL-terminated string the function borrows for the call is a borrowed C
  string, or the Rust string or path type of the encoding the analysis establishes,
  converted at the call, an interior NUL rejected before it. A returned string is a borrow
  tied to what keeps it alive, or an owner over its releaser where the caller frees it.
- **Nullability.** A nullable pointer is an `Option`.
- **Errors.** A function that can fail returns a `Result`, its failure read from the error
  convention the analysis establishes: a status return, a sentinel return, or error state
  the library keeps beside the call, read immediately after it, before another call into
  the library can replace it. Error state a failure sets and only a caller clears, such as
  a sticky error flag, tells the call's failure by its change alone, with nothing else able
  to change it in between. A return that reports only success is not returned, and an
  outcome its C callers treat as ordinary, such as an exhausted iteration or an absent
  entry, is part of the success value. Each error convention has one error type, carrying
  what the convention reports, `errno`'s being `std::io::Error`.
- **Variadics.** A variadic function is bound through fixed-arity forms: one that formats
  its arguments takes the formatted message, passed to a `"%s"` format, and any other is
  one function per argument list its callers use. A `va_list` function is reached only
  through its variadic sibling.

A `static inline` function a header defines is bound as an exported one is: it is
allowlisted, and called through the raw binding generated for it, as
[`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Generation section describes. The exception is a short
one whose whole implementation is in the header, which may be ported instead, to save the
cost of an FFI call, unless what it does depends on the build's features or configuration.
A reimplementation is a port, as [`porting`](../../porting/SKILL.md) describes, and is
annotated `Replaces`, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Anchors section describes.

Moved (exclusively or refcounted), borrowed (immutably or mutably), nullable, scalar and
array variants are separate functions when one signature cannot express every valid
contract. A function taking or returning type-erased arguments is generic.

A method is emitted in an `impl T` block on the type it implements, taking `&self` or
`&mut self` as its first argument. A free function stays free.

## 2. Globals

A global is bound as a `'static` borrow, never as an owner, its value taking the safe form
its type takes in a signature, as [Functions](#1-functions) describes. Its access
discipline follows from every C access:

- immutable after initialization: a shared handle;
- synchronized by C: the matching safe synchronization (an atomic, or guards handing out
  the shared or exclusive handle under the lock), never discarding a lock's status;
- otherwise mutable: `unsafe` accessors that exclude concurrent access, reported as such;
- thread-local: a handle borrowed for a closure on the current thread, neither `Send` nor
  `Sync`.

A lock counts only if every access takes it and it rejects same-thread re-entry. A global
C sets up in a routine, rather than in its definition, is reached through the safe API only
once that routine has run, however the binding ensures it.

## 3. Function pointers

A function pointer is bound from its declaration and every site that calls it or supplies
it, a function assigned to it or passed as it. One a typedef declares is named after its
typedef; one written inline is named after the site that declares it, the field,
parameter, return or global, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming
section describes, so that two inline pointers of one signature in one file are two items
when their sites differ.
<!-- TODO: wavefront keys an inline function pointer by its signature and home file, so
the sites of one signature in one file are one item; it has yet to key them by declaring
site, a local's or a cast's folded into the site whose value it carries. -->

It is bound to a safe callable type that holds either of its implementations:

- a Rust closure, which C reaches through a trampoline of the C signature and the context
  C passes back to it; and
- a C function, with its context, which Rust calls: made only inside the crate, through an
  `unsafe` constructor whose contract states what the C that supplies it guarantees, the
  function's validity and its context's lifetime and threads, and safe to call, its
  arguments and result converted as a function's binding converts them.

A function pointer that crosses the boundary gets both, whichever direction its uses take
today, since a port turns the C that calls or supplies it into Rust, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section describes, and its safe API
does not change then. Its consumers see only the safe form, its closures taking and
returning safe types: a closure borrowed for the call, `impl FnMut(…)`, where C keeps it
for the call that receives it; an owned closure, released with its context, where C keeps
it until it releases it; and a trait, for a struct of function pointers a library calls
into, which Rust types and the C implementation implement alike. A function pointer read
from C, such as a field's getter returns, is the callable type, never the raw pointer.
How long C keeps it is a finding of the analysis.

Its trampoline is a panic barrier, which maps a panic to the C's error convention, and it
refuses a re-entrant call, which would alias an `FnMut` closure, unless the analysis shows
that C re-enters it, which takes an `Fn` closure instead. A function pointer C calls from
another thread takes a `Send` closure, and a `Sync` one when C may call it from several at
once. Three cases shape the type further:

- one without a context parameter carries no captured state: its Rust implementation is a
  closure without captures, each closure type its own trampoline, or a plain function;
- one C reads as absent when null, where it uses a default or calls nothing, is an
  `Option` of the callable type; and
- one C compares with a known function, such as its default implementation, keeps in its C
  variant the pointer it was made from, so that the comparison still holds.

When its sites hand ownership across differently, each distribution has its own distinctly
named callable type over the one C function-pointer type.

## 4. Macros

A C macro is bound to a Rust form of its own:

- a type-generating macro, to one generic type, through [`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md),
  its instances aliases of it;
- a constant macro, to a `const`, defined from its generated binding;
- a symbol alias, through the safe wrapper of the symbol it names, each of whose stand-ins
  stands in for the alias too and carries its anchor beside the symbol's own: where the
  symbol is a lifecycle primitive, the strategy methods that call it, as
  [Lifecycle strategies](#5-lifecycle-strategies) describes; and
- a macro that implements logic, to a function, `#[inline]`, or `const` where its body
  computes on its arguments alone, which reimplements the body and reaches C only for the
  symbols its expansion uses, through their safe wrappers, and for the fields it accesses,
  through their accessors. A `macro_rules!` takes its place only where a function cannot
  express it: control flow that leaves its caller, token pasting or stringification, an
  argument used as a place, or one evaluated lazily or more than once.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration, which the Rust does not see,
is the exception: it is reached through a shim, `crustify_<NAME>`, bound and wrapped.

## 5. Lifecycle strategies

A type's own lifecycle routines are bound with the type, as
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section describes. The foundational
modules hold the rest: the allocators or constructors, releasers, disposers and cloners of
type-erased memory and of strings, each with the lifecycle role established while
planning, as [`decomposition`](../../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational
modules section describes. The analysis confirms each role from the item's body, and a role
the body contradicts is corrected, the correction recorded with the batch.

In a foundational module's batch, an item with a lifecycle role becomes a generic policy
or strategy that calls the primitive, through which the owners of strings and of
type-erased singletons and arrays allocate, clone and release what they hold, so that each
owner frees what it holds through the family that allocated it. The primitive itself is
not also exposed as an ordinary safe function. The module's other items follow their
route.

Singleton and array handles have separate policies, each in its primitive's home. A
family's allocator, releaser and cloner form one policy. A releaser that frees a container together with its
elements is no policy of the container: where its body only releases each element and then
the container, the owner holds its elements as their own owners, under the container's
allocator's policy, and releases as the releaser does without calling it; where it does
more, the owner is hand-written.

# Soundness patterns

The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the

Equivalence tests section describes.

hold, and reports which in its final message, as

bindings.

# ffibox

ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its

primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A

# Wave 3's write through a shared stream handle takes the stream's lock itself

Status: `landed`, as the alternative its Destination names, in glibc-crustify
`wave-3/batch-0/run-1`'s landing (2026-11-13): `flockfile` and `funlockfile` are bound
privately inside `fprintf`'s module, as the lock its one call takes, and the plan does not
change. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-2/batch-0/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the default
`repair` autonomy (`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` gives no `evolution` answer): a correction to a
campaign artifact the planner owns, proposed.

## Signal

A plan that would ask a later batch for a binding its analysis cannot make sound
(`evolution` §2, "plan corrections"). Planner run 1 (`25b3fe2`) plans `fprintf` (wave 3) as
`fprintf(stream, "%s", message)` through `_IO_FILE`'s shared handle, on the ground that
"glibc locks every stream operation, which the binder confirms before a shared handle
writes". Wave 2's analysis does not confirm it for every stream:

- `vfprintf` (`c/stdio-common/vfprintf-internal.c:1540-1563`) locks with the
  `_IO_flockfile` macro, which `c/libio/libio.h:282` makes a no-op when the stream carries
  `_IO_USER_LOCK`. `__fsetlocking(fp, FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER)` sets that flag
  (`c/libio/__fsetlocking.c:31-32`). Native code, not Rust, sets it.
- `flockfile` (`c/stdio-common/flockfile.c`) takes the stream's lock (`_IO_lock_lock`) with
  no flag check, and the lock is recursive (`sysdeps/nptl/stdio-lock.h`: owner and count).
  So `fprintf` called inside `flockfile`/`funlockfile` is serialized whatever the stream's
  locking mode.

`File`'s `Sync` (`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`, wave 2) therefore rests on this rule: every
operation bound on `FileRef` holds the stream's lock, taken with `flockfile`, for the
whole of its access. A `Sync` that relied on the stream's locking mode would rest on data
the native code can change, which `binding`'s Safe boundary section forbids.

## Destination

A campaign artifact: `modules.json` and `schedule.json`, the planner's. `flockfile` and
`funlockfile` (`stdio-common/flockfile.c`, `stdio-common/funlockfile.c`, declared in
`libio/stdio.h`) join the plan ahead of wave 3, or in its batch, since wave 3's `fprintf`
binding needs them. They could also be bound privately inside `fprintf`'s module, as the
lock its one call takes, with no public API of their own.

## Change

Planner run 2 adds the two functions as items wave 3 reaches. The fixed-arity form stays
as planned: `flockfile(stream)`, `fprintf(stream, "%s", message)`, `funlockfile(stream)`,
with the count returned, or `errno`'s `io::Error` on a negative return.

## Validation

Wave 3's binder confirmed it from `fprintf`'s analysis, and the assistant's task message
settled the destination: the two routines are raw bindings in `fprintf.rs`'s `ffi_import`,
allowlisted, with no safe API. `FileRef::print` holds the lock from before `fprintf` to
after `errno` is read. Two unit tests show that the lock is what serializes the writes
(`tests/unit_pub/fprintf.rs`). `writes_from_threads_never_interleave` shares one handle
among 8 threads on a `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER` stream. It passes, and with the binding's
`flockfile` and `funlockfile` removed it fails three runs in three with interleaved lines
(an `open_memstream` stream aborts in glibc instead).
`print_waits_for_the_lock_on_a_stream_locked_by_its_caller` passes, and with them removed
it sees the waiting thread's text written first. No consumer of the parent campaigns needs
the lock routines as API of their own: `cli_opt_status_fprint`, `spec_name_fprint` and
`llhttp__debug` each make one `fprintf` per message.

# `stderr()` lends a `FileRef<'static>` from safe code, on assumptions about the program's C that the crate cannot check

- **item**: `glb::stderr`, bound as `stderr() -> FileRef<'static>`,
  `src/libc/libio/stdio.rs`: the two `// SAFETY:` justifications of its `ffi_import` body
  and the safe signature they let it keep
- **affected commit**: `2a792a8` (wave 4, batch 0)
- **objective**: `contracts`, of the `ffi_import` region. A safe function discharges
  `FileRef::from_ptr`'s contract for the `'static` lifetime by assuming what the whole
  program's C does with a variable glibc lets it set. The contract breaks through safe
  code. The reproducer below shows a heap-use-after-free under ASan.

## What is wrong

`stderr()` is safe and returns `FileRef<'static>`. Its body reads the global `stderr` and
borrows the stream it names with `FileRef::from_ptr`, whose contract for a stream
(`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`, `File`'s documentation, as `6e892ea` corrected it) is:

> the pointer is NULL or an open stream that stays open for the handle's lifetime, `fclose`
> included, and every other access to it while the handle lives, C's or Rust's, on any
> thread, holds its lock.

For `'static`, the function discharges this with assumptions about the program, which its
doc lists. No code assigns `stderr` while another thread may read it. Nothing passes its
stream to `fclose` or to a failing `freopen`. Its locking stays internal. The doc and the
batch's commit message justify these by what glibc's own routines and the C of the two
parent campaigns do. They do not follow from anything the crate or the C contract
guarantees:

- glibc's `stderr` is a variable a program may set. Its manual (`c/manual/stdio.texi:115-122`)
  says so: "In the GNU C Library, `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr` are normal variables which
  you can set just like any others." It gives `fclose (stdout); stdout = fopen (…);` as
  the way to redirect a standard stream.
- A stream so opened is heap memory that `fclose` frees. `_IO_new_fclose` ends in
  `_IO_deallocate_file` (`c/libio/iofclose.c:74`), which spares only `_IO_2_1_stdin_`,
  `_IO_2_1_stdout_` and `_IO_2_1_stderr_` and frees every other stream
  (`c/libio/libioP.h:948-958`). Even `_IO_2_1_stderr_` is closed by `fclose`, and C11
  7.21.3p4 leaves a closed stream's pointer indeterminate.
- The handle is `Copy`, `Send` and `'static`, so safe code may keep it anywhere: in a
  `static`, as the batch's own `ub_safe` test `the_handle_outlives_every_scope` does, or on
  a detached thread. C's own `fprintf (stderr, …)` reads the variable at each call. A kept
  Rust handle does not, so a program that redirects its standard error stream is correct C
  and still leaves the handle dangling.

`glibc-bindings` is a library. It is linked into programs whose C it cannot see, and the
parents' C is not all of that C either: libgit2 is itself a library. `binding-symbols`'
Globals section binds a global by its C accesses. A global that is neither immutable after
initialization nor synchronized by C is "otherwise mutable", and gets `unsafe` accessors
that exclude concurrent access. ffibox's goals (`docs/goals.md`, G9 and G10) exclude use
after free through lifetimes, and make adopting a pointer `unsafe`, "an unknown fact
selects[ing] the more restrictive primitive". The safe `'static` signature does neither.

The read of the global has the same flaw: its `// SAFETY:` comment excludes a racing
write by assuming the program makes none. Since glibc lets a program write `stderr`, the
crate cannot vouch for that from safe code.

No safe operation on `FileRef` reads the stream yet in this tree. Wave 3's `FileRef::print`
(`stdio-common/fprintf.c`, on its own branch) will take the handle's stream lock with
`flockfile` and then call `fprintf`. Once both land, `stderr().print(…)` on a kept handle is
a use after free in safe code. The reproducer makes that operation's first read itself,
in Rust, where ASan sees it, since glibc is not instrumented.

## Reproducer

`reproducer/`, a standalone package over the affected crate. It is single-threaded, and
each C step is one glibc's manual offers, written in Rust through extern declarations as C
would make it:

1. C redirects `stderr` to a stream it opens: `stderr = fopen("/dev/null", "w")`.
2. Safe Rust takes `let kept: FileRef<'static> = stderr();`.
3. C rotates it: `fclose(stderr); stderr = <the original stream>`.
4. `kept` is still a live `'static` handle. ASan reports its stream freed
   (`__asan_address_is_poisoned`), and the read that `flockfile`, `FileRef::print`'s first
   step, makes of the stream's `_lock` is a heap-use-after-free.

**Verdict: rejected.** It needs two fixes, and both can be made by removing text. Nothing was changed, committed or landed, no gate or rerun was run, and I wrote no scratch files.

The change does answer the signal. Its first two sentences fix the misreading behind the finding: the accesses that decide are those the C contract allows, not only those the campaign's C makes. It sits in the right place. `porting-symbols`' Globals section defers to this section, so ports pick the rule up too. It states no rule in the target's names: "libc's standard streams" is only an example, the way `binding` already uses libc. It touches no protected path.

The validation matches what the proposal says, read without a rerun:
- the fix commit `a5448ee` is there;
- `stderr` on `crustify/devel` is `pub unsafe fn stderr<'a>() -> FileRef<'a>`;
- `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/stdio_stderr_is_lent_by_no_safe_code.rs` exists;
- planner run 2's plan correction is cited.

The change is independent of `a3552fb`, which touches a different file. If `a3552fb` is rejected, rebasing this commit onto `e8e55af` falls under the text-only rebase exception and needs no new review.

## Required fixes

1. **Remove the "safe operation" alternative.** It contradicts other rules, and the validation does not support it.
   - **The section's own list.** The paragraph classes the global as "otherwise mutable". The list says such a global gets "`unsafe` accessors that exclude concurrent access". The paragraph then allows a safe operation on it ("a safe accessor never lends that beyond one call: either the accessor is `unsafe`…, or a safe operation…"). A binder and a reviewer reading the two would reach opposite results.
   - **The lock rule.** "Holding the lock C takes there" points at a lock the next paragraph says does not count, because it allows same-thread re-entry. glibc's stream lock is recursive. ffibox's `ownership.md:188` also says a guard's lock must not be recursive.
   - **The finding itself.** The finding says the crate "cannot vouch" from safe code that the read of the global does not race. The validated fix stays `unsafe` even for a one-call handle. Nothing in the validation exercises a safe operation.
   - **The fix.** Delete "a safe accessor never lends that beyond one call: either" and ", or a safe operation reads the global and uses what it names within the call, holding the lock C takes there". The sentence becomes: "…the C that reassigns it may free what it pointed to, so the accessor is `unsafe`, its caller vouching for the lifetime it chooses."
2. **Fix the record row.**
   - **The recurrence signal reads "a `ub` finding".** The original finding was filed under `contracts`, so a recurrence filed the same way would not meet the signal and would go unfiled. Remove "`ub`".
   - **The "change" column** says "a safe accessor never lends what it points to beyond a call". After fix 1 it should say "its accessor is unsafe".

## Agreement with soundness and ffibox

- **soundness.** Once fix 1 is made, the rule agrees with the `soundness` skill:
  - its `hidden-dependency` pattern already names "a global the program may close", and the rule matches what that pattern says prevents it;
  - it also agrees with `unsynchronised-global`, since the Rust cannot serialise the program's writes. That pattern is another reason to drop the safe-operation clause.
- **ffibox.** The paragraph names no ffibox primitive. It is consistent with ffibox's docs:
  - `CGuardedRef` is for a global that is never released, under one non-recursive lock (`borrows.md`, `ownership.md:188`, `:295`);
  - `goals.md` G10 says an unknown fact selects the more restrictive primitive, which supports the `unsafe` accessor.

## Does it weaken a check?

No check in the Review section's sense. The safe-operation clause does loosen the "otherwise mutable → `unsafe`" rule that reviewers judge bindings against, without saying so. Fix 1 removes that clause.

## Not required

- **The proposal quotes a different text from the commit.** Its Change section has "not those" where the commit has "not only those". It names `environ` and `optarg`, and "as the C expression does", which the commit dropped. It should quote the commit before it lands, so the record is accurate.
- **The signal is filed under the wrong row of the signals table.** It cites "a rule the how-to skills lack", which is the row for findings that recur. The evidence, one finding plus a plan correction, fits "leads its agent wrong" and "plan corrections" better.
- **"A global is bound as a `'static` borrow"** could be sharpened to say it is the global's storage that is borrowed for `'static`, not what a pointer global points to.
- **"The C that reassigns it may free"** misses a `fclose` with no reassignment. "Closes or reassigns" would cover it.
- **A gap that would add a rule:** whether a non-`const` public global that the docs never mention counts as "one a program may set".
- **A citation that would add text:** the paragraph could name `soundness`' `hidden-dependency`.

I proposed, changed and recorded nothing. This run changes and lands nothing, and nothing in it called for a proposal.
